catalog_quote: L'accent, placé généralement sur la dernière syllabe des mots, peut être, en fonction de l'ajout de morphèmes, à l'initiale, au milieu d'un mot ou en finale. L'accent peut distinguer les paires de mots : dərə́ 'vallée' / də́r=ə 'porte=ACC' [...] xunə́ 'maison' / xún=ə 'sang=ACC'. Certaines particules, conjonctions ou adverbes ont l'accent sur la première syllabe : kítam 'quel(le)', çícür 'comment', bə́lkə 'peut-être' [...] Dans les mots formés d'un nom suivi du suffixe de comparatif, d'un suffixe de pluriel ou d'un suffixe de dérivation nominal, l'accent tombe sur celui-ci : cuqlə-tə́ 'plus petit', zən-ún 'femmes', tərsi-rə-lǘ 'effrayant'. Dans les noms composés, l'accent est généralement placé sur la dernière syllabe du second élément [...] Les groupes nominaux sont accentués sur la dernière syllabe du dernier élément : sibi rúş 'barbe blanche' [...] Dans les mots qui portent les enclitiques =(r)ə d'accusatif, =(ə)m de focus, =gə d'altérité et l'ézâfé, l'accent tombe sur la syllabe qui précède ces enclitiques : márə 'le serpent', ayóləm 'l'enfant aussi', yətə́gə 'l'autre', víni 'le nez de'. Les préverbes, le morphème de négation et le préfixe du prohibitif attirent l'accent : fúdərən 'couvrir', nə́deyşirənum 'je ne regarde pas' [...] Il en va de même pour les préfixes bI= du subjonctif, ye= du futur et mI= de l'éventuel : bíyam 'que je vienne' [...]

new_statements.translation: Stress, generally placed on the last syllable of words, may, depending on the addition of morphemes, be initial, word-medial or final. Stress can distinguish word pairs: dərə́ 'valley' / də́r=ə 'door=ACC' [...] In words formed from a noun plus the comparative suffix, a plural suffix or a nominal derivational suffix, stress falls on that suffix: cuqlə-tə́ 'smaller', zən-ún 'women' [...] In words carrying the enclitics =(r)ə accusative, =(ə)m focus, =gə alterity and the ezafe, stress falls on the syllable preceding these enclitics [...] Preverbs, the negation morpheme and the prohibitive prefix attract the stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is final in the (suffixed) word: bare stems and stems plus plural/comparative/derivational suffixes are stressed on the last syllable; case/focus/alterity enclitics and the ezafe are extrametrical (stress stays on the last pre-clitic syllable, hence pairs like dərə́ vs də́r=ə); in verbs, preverbs, negation nə-, prohibitive mə- and the TAM prefixes bI=/ye=/mI= pull stress to the prefix; a closed set of particles/adverbs (kítam, bə́lkə..) and bi- privative adjectives are initial-stressed. Grjunberg 1997 §2.1.2 (p. 144) gives the same final-stress rule for Tat generally (expiratory stress, last syllable of nouns; plural suffix stressed, case endings unstressed; negation takes main stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mammadova: none stated. Grjunberg 1997 p. 144: in two-component verb forms main stress on the lexical component, secondary on the auxiliary; under negation main stress moves to the negative prefix and a secondary stress remains on the originally stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial stress on certain particles/conjunctions/adverbs (kítam 'which', çícür 'how', bə́lkə 'perhaps', ázru, bádə, hə́rçi, xéyli, sǘfdi, míyanə, bíqey), on indefinites/demonstratives hər, hiç, i, u in phrases (hə́r cegə, híçkes, íncə), on the privative prefix bi- (bíaqül), on both members' first syllable in reduplicated adjectives/adverbs (búrmə-búrmə); verbal prefixes (preverbs, negation, prohibitive, subjunctive bI=, future ye=, eventual mI=) attract stress; enclitics and ezafe unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description with citation forms; also states noun phrases are stressed on the last syllable of their last element (sibi rúş 'white beard'). Variety described is Absheron (Apsheron) Tat, spoken Muslim Tat of the Baku area (Glottolog dialect absh1238 under musl1236).
new_statements.identity_note: Primary quote describes Absheron (Apsheron) Tat, the Muslim Tat of the Baku peninsula villages (Balakhany, Surakhany etc.), Glottolog dialect absh1238 under musl1236. The supporting Russian statement (Grjunberg 1997, p. 144) is framed for 'Tat' as a whole but the author says (p. 142) his description is based on the northern dialect (Judeo-Tat jude1256 / Armeno-Tat), the southern = Muslim dialects being treated only in §2.7.0, which does not mention stress; both sources agree on final stress.

sources.note: §1.3.4 Accentuation, pp. 14-15: stress generally on the last syllable of the word; plural, comparative and nominal derivational suffixes take the stress; case/focus/alterity enclitics and the ezafe leave stress on the preceding syllable; preverbs, negation, prohibitive and TAM prefixes (bI=, ye=, mI=) attract stress; some particles/adverbs and bi- privative adjectives are initial-stressed; minimal pairs dərə́ 'valley' vs də́r=ə 'door=ACC'.

sources.note: §2.1.2, p. 144: 'Ударение эскпираторное [sic]. В именах, не осложненных словоизменительными морфемами, падает на последний слог'; plural suffix stressed, case endings unstressed; finite verbs: stress on stem (past), on first syllable (imperative, subjunctive), or on ending (present/future/perfect); negation takes main stress; stressed vowels are longer. NB p. 142 states the description is based on the northern (Judeo-Tat/Armeno-Tat) dialect, with southern (Muslim) dialect notes in §2.7.0, which say nothing about stress.
